## Three Questions Before Every Task

1. **Which tool?** Decide by data sensitivity first, convenience second.
2. **Which model?** Decide by task size: start medium, go down if the task is mechanical, go up only when the smaller model fails.
3. **Which setting?** Decide how much context the agent needs from you:
   - **A good prompt** is enough for a one-off task: name the file, the goal and what not to touch.
   - **A memory file** for work you keep doing in the same project: language, folders, key variable names.
   - **A skill** for instructions you reuse across projects, or have pasted three times.

::: {.fragment}
And keep the habit from earlier: a new session for each new task.
:::

## What Counts as a New Task?

**Ask yourself:** does my next request need anything from *this conversation* (beyond what is already in my files or memory file?)

- **No → new session.** The earlier discussion would just make your chat more expensive without adding anything. 
- **Yes → stay.** The agent needs what you just worked out together.

::: {.fragment}
| Example | Same task or new? |
|---|---|
| Draft slide 5, then fix a typo on slide 5 | **Same** -- builds directly on the same slide |
| Draft slide 5, then draft slide 9 on a different topic | **New** -- only the style carries over, and that belongs in a memory file or skill |
| Debug a regression, then write the README | **New** -- Even if it's for the same project, there is no need for context beyond the files and memory file 
| Summarize the Kenya country report, then the Uganda report with the same instructions | **New** -- reuse the prompt, not the chat |
:::

## Step 1: Which Tool?

| Tool | Use it for | Data you may share |
|---|---|---|
| **GitHub Copilot** | Code in VS Code: writing, debugging, refactoring | WBG work, up to official use only |
| **Claude Enterprise** | Same with more level of security + Documents, reports, long analyses, Claude Code | WBG work, up to confidential |
| **mAI** | Everyday writing, summaries, quick questions | WBG work, up to strictly confidential |
| **M365 Copilot** | Word drafts, PowerPoint slides, email and meeting summaries | WBG work, up to strictly confidential |
| **Personal Claude / ChatGPT** | Learning with public material | **Public information only** |

::: {.fragment}
- M365 Copilot have no per-user limit -- great for writing, but "no limit for you" is not "free for the Bank" so also have cost-effectiveness practices in mind. mAI just implemented cap (35 USD) for advanced models (Sonnet/Opus/Sol).
:::

## Step 2: Which Model? -- Cheat Sheet

| Tier | Use it for | Research economist examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Small**<br>Haiku, GPT Luna | Mechanical, well-specified tasks | Proofread an abstract, rename variables, reformat a table |
| **Medium** -- *default*<br>Sonnet, GPT Terra | Most everyday work | Translate Stata to R, debug a regression script, compare two documents |
| **Large**<br>Opus, GPT Sol | Many files, or ambiguous problems | Review a full reproducibility package, critique an identification strategy |

::: {.fragment}
**Escalate, don't default.** If the small model gets it right, keep using it.
:::


# Case Study: An Afternoon on the Cash Plus RCT {background-color="#530153"}

## The Setup

A (fictional) impact evaluation: cash transfers plus nutrition coaching in rural Kenya, 60 villages, 1,200 households.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The project folder**

- R scripts: clean, balance table, ITT regressions
- Baseline and endline survey data
- Pre-analysis plan, field notes, two old paper drafts
- The current abstract
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Three everyday tasks**

1. Fix the balance table script (it crashes on wrong variable names)
2. Proofread the abstract
3. Write a README
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note}
- We ran the same three tasks three ways in Claude Code and recorded every token.
- We ran it using claude personal and enterprise and the results are the same, with some differences on specific tokens 
as that will always vary from run to run. The reported results are using Claude Enterprise. 
:::

## Three Workflows, Three Costs

| | **A: One chat** | **B: New session per task** | **C: All three habits** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 1 for all tasks | 1 per task | 1 per task |
| Memory file | No | No | Yes |
| Prompts | Vague: "The balance table isn't working. Can you fix it?" | Same vague prompts | Specific: names the file, the error and what not to touch |
| Model | Opus for everything | Opus for everything | Sonnet to debug, Haiku to proofread and write the README |

## The Memory File We Used for C {#memory-file-c}

<style>#memory-file-c pre code { font-size: 19px !important; line-height: 1.3 !important; }</style>

```markdown
# Cash Plus RCT
Cluster RCT of cash transfers + nutrition coaching in rural Kenya.
60 villages (30 treated), 1,200 households. Randomized at village level.

## Language and packages
- R only: dplyr, fixest, here. Paths built with `here::here()`.

## Folder structure
- `code/00_main.R`: runs everything in order (01_clean → 02_balance → 03_analysis)
- `data/raw/`: `baseline_hh.csv`, `endline_hh.csv` (merge on `hhid`)
- `docs/`: pre-analysis plan, field notes, old drafts. Don't read unless asked.

## Data
- Source: household surveys, baseline (2024) and endline (2025). De-identified; can be shared.
- Every README must include a data availability statement.

## Key variable names
- Treatment: `treatment` (0/1). Cluster: `village_id`. ID: `hhid`.
- Baseline: `hh_size`, `head_female`, `head_educ_yrs`, `consumption_pc`, ...
```

Five minutes to write with a lot of impact (you will see). (You can also us an Agent to write it, Haiku model would be enough.)

## The Case Study, Live {#live-demo}

<style>#live-demo pre code { font-size: 28px !important; line-height: 1.4 !important; }</style>

```bash
cd case-study
python3 run_case.py
```

- Everything is in the `case-study/` folder next to these slides: the project, the memory file and the script. You can run it yourself.
- Each workflow gets a fresh copy of `cashplus-project/`, with the broken balance table, the typos and the empty README.
- I'll run it now (about 4 minutes). Then we'll open what each workflow produced: the fixed code, the proofread abstract and the README.

::: {.fragment}
Your numbers will not match ours exactly: the agent takes a slightly different path every time. A is always the most expensive.
:::

## The Results

Input tokens processed per task, from our run on Claude Enterprise (including tokens resent from earlier in the conversation):

| Task | **A: One chat** | **B: New sessions** | **C: All habits** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Fix the balance table | 145k | 127k | 56k |
| Proofread the abstract | 229k | 48k | 58k |
| Write a README | 300k | 158k | 78k |
| **Total** | **675k** | **333k** | **191k** |
| **Cost** | **$0.65** | **$0.43** | **$0.05** | 

::: {.fragment}
- **C used just over a quarter of A's tokens and cost 12x less**, because it also ran on smaller models.
- **Did it work?** All three fixed the balance table. A and C fixed all 8 typos; B only listed them. All three wrote a README, but only C's says where the data come from and how to access them, because the memory file asks for it.
:::

## What Drove the Difference

::: {.fragment}
- **New task.** The *same prompt*, "Can you proofread the abstract?", cost 229k tokens as the second task in a long chat and 48k in a fresh one: almost 5x, only from carrying task 1 along.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- **Setting.** Without a memory file, the agents in A and B read the pre-analysis plan and the field notes, which none of the tasks needed. With it, the agent in C opened 4 small files plus the header row of the data.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- **Model.** Haiku proofread the abstract and wrote the README without problems. Neither task needed Opus.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- **Vague prompts are a coin toss.** Asked only to "proofread", A fixed the typos but B just listed them, so a real user would need one more turn. The specific prompt said "edit the file", and C did.
:::

## Read the Numbers 

- **One run per workflow.** Runs vary: tasks A1 and B1 had identical setups and still differed by 14% (145k vs 127k).
- **Claude Code has a floor.** Every request sends a large set of built-in instructions, so even the shortest task cost ~50k tokens here. Chat tools start lower, but the patterns are the same.
- **The project is fictional and small.** This grows with every task you add to a chat, so on a real project with longer chats the gap tends to widen.

::: {.fragment}
The scripts to rerun this case study are in `case-study/` next to these slides.
:::

# 5-Minute Homework: Where Am I Wasting Tokens? {background-color="#530153"}

## Step 1: Self-Audit (5 Minutes, No AI Needed)

Open your chat history in Visual Studio/Claude Code and look at your **last 10 chats**. Count how many had:

- [ ] **A very long thread**: several tasks, or the same job repeated on file after file, in one chat (the trailers)
- [ ] **Three or more corrections**, such as "no, I meant...", before you got what you wanted
- [ ] **A large paste or attachment** when only one section mattered
- [ ] **A vague first prompt** that the agent had to explore or ask about
- [ ] **A large model** for a small task, such as proofreading or reformatting
- [ ] **The same prompt** that you have typed or pasted before

## Step 2: Ask the AI (Optional)

In **Claude/Claude Enterprise** or **GitHub Copilot**, start a **new chat** with a **small model** (Haiku) or **medium** (Sonnet), and paste:

> Review my recent chats and identify the ones that likely used the most tokens, and why: for example, long threads covering several tasks, repeated corrections, large pastes or attachments, vague first prompts, or a large model used for a simple task. For each one, suggest one specific change that would make it more efficient, such as starting a new chat, writing a clearer first prompt, using a smaller model, or turning a repeated prompt into a project or skill. Skip chats that were already short and focused. Return a table with the columns **Chat**, **Why it was expensive**, and **Suggested change**.


## Step 3: Think About It

- What was your most common waste pattern?
- Which one change would save you the most?
- Did anything show up repeatedly that should become a **project, skill, or script**?

::: {.fragment}
**Rule of thumb:** a prompt you have pasted three times is a skill waiting to be written.
:::
